copy.blurb:
A +7.8pp gap on the Scotland side. Scotland v Brazil in FIFA World Cup 2026 is the match. The model has Scotland stronger than the market does — that's the reason this fires as a Pick rather than a Pass.

On Elo, Brazil comes in 220 points ahead — Scotland at 1750, Brazil at 1970. Both Elo numbers are pulled live from the public Elo source. The adjustment layer is quiet on this fixture — no host bonus, no home-ground correction, no altitude folding in. The Elo numbers above are what the model uses.

Three-way split from the model: Scotland to win at 18%, the draw at 17%, and Brazil to win at 65%. The home side reads 18% on this distribution — the model's central case for Scotland.

On the same three-way, Kalshi: Scotland to win at 10%, the draw at 18%, and Brazil to win at 72%. Kalshi has Scotland at 10%, which prices out at American odds of +852; the model has the same side at 18%. The +7.8pp gap across them is the disagreement we're surfacing.

Bootstrap discipline matters most on the longshots — wide bands on small point estimates collapse the Pick rate fast. On Scotland the lower bound is 14%, which keeps the lower-bound gap at +3.9pp against the market — past +3pp, so the Pick clears. The claim is narrow: on this fixture, on this side, the price is below what the underlying read supports. We don't argue the market is broadly wrong — across the priced field the model and the line agree more often than they disagree. We surface the ones where they don't.

What would close this gap: confirmed team news that pulls the prior down on the side we like, a venue or weather change, or a tournament suspension landing before kickoff. With kickoff 29 days out, refresh is weekly; daily cadence picks up inside the final five days. A Pick this wide doesn't collapse on small news; a narrow one can flip to Pass on a single refresh. Either way, the engine republishes and the page reflects the latest read. Per The Guardian (football): "He will be an important player in this World Cup."
